docs.title: Architectural Challenge
docs.text:
In modern enterprise environments, engineering teams require secure, seamless access to sensitive cloud workloads spanning development, staging, and production environments across multiple AWS Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) and on-premises datacenters.

Traditionally, organizations relied on Bastion Jump Hosts or Self-Managed EC2 VPN Concentrators. However, these legacy architectures introduce critical enterprise liabilities:

Vulnerabilities of Legacy Ingress Models

  • Public Attack Surface: Publicly exposed SSH (port 22) or RDP (port 3389) endpoints invite brute-force scanning, port probes, and zero-day exploitation.
  • Credential Leakage & Stale Keys: Static SSH private keys or shared VPN certificate files distributed across developer laptops cannot be cleanly or immediately revoked upon employee offboarding.
  • Unrestricted Lateral Movement: Once perimeter ingress is breached, an attacker frequently gains broad Layer 3 access to adjacent subnets and resources due to a lack of identity-aware network segmentation.
  • Operational Overhead & Scaling Bottlenecks: Self-hosted OpenVPN servers on EC2 require manual OS patching, licensing, manual failover clustering, and bandwidth resizing.

docs.title: Zero-Trust Solution
docs.text: AWS Client VPN delivers an elastic, fully managed, client-based VPN service based on the open-source OpenVPN protocol. It replaces fragmented jump hosts with a unified, identity-aware ingress architecture.

docs.title: Value Proposition Matrix
docs.text: Architectural Pillar Legacy Jump Host / EC2 VPN AWS Client VPN Managed Service High Availability Manual active/passive clustering; single point of failure Automated multi-AZ elasticity backed by AWS infrastructure Authentication Static SSH keys or local Linux users Federated SAML 2.0 (Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, IAM Identity Center) with MFA Authorization All-or-nothing subnet routing Granular, group-based network ingress rules mapped to Directory groups Traffic Path Full tunnel or complex manual iptables routing Configurable split-tunneling; non-corporate traffic bypasses AWS Logging & Audit Local /var/log/secure logs requiring custom forwarders Native Amazon CloudWatch connection logging and CloudTrail audit trails

docs.title: Key Design Tenets
docs.text:
1. Identity-Driven Perimeter: User authentication happens prior to network packet forwarding. Unauthenticated packets are dropped at the edge.
  2. Stateful Security Group Chaining: Traffic leaving the Client VPN endpoint carries an AWS Security Group ID. Target applications accept traffic only from the Client VPN security group, completely ignoring arbitrary IP ranges.
  3. Split-Tunnel Optimization: Corporate traffic is selectively pushed over the secure tunnel, while standard internet traffic (video streaming, general web browsing) remains on the client's local internet breakout, preserving AWS egress bandwidth and minimizing latency.
  4. Deterministic Observability: Every connection attempt, termination, source IP, duration, and data volume is captured natively in Amazon CloudWatch Logs for compliance and forensics.

docs.title: Documentation Roadmap
docs.text:
To thoroughly evaluate and implement this architecture, review the structured sections in this guide:

  • Network Fundamentals: Deep-dive into VPC design, CIDR allocation, Subnet sizing, Route Tables, and Elastic Network Interfaces (ENI).
  • AWS Client VPN Core: Endpoint specifications, packet flow lifecycle, SAML 2.0 federated identity, and security hardening.
  • Enterprise Use Cases: Architectural topologies covering Single VPC, Multi-VPC Peering, Transit Gateway, and Hybrid Cloud.
  • Operations & Governance: Observability metrics, log forensics, and architecture FAQs.

docs.title: AWS Client VPN Service Architecture & Endpoints
Overview
docs.text: AWS Client VPN is an enterprise-managed, elastic VPN service designed to grant remote engineers secure, TLS-encrypted access to AWS VPC resources, multi-VPC topologies, and hybrid on-premises environments.

docs.title: Architectural Components
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Client["Remote Engineer Client<br/>(AWS Client VPN / OpenVPN Client)"] -->|TLS VPN Session| Endpoint["AWS Client VPN Endpoint<br/>(Elastic Managed Gateway)"]

    subgraph AuthenticationLayer ["Authentication Layer"]
        SAML["SAML 2.0 IdP<br/>(Entra ID / Okta / IAM Identity Center)"]
        mTLS["Mutual TLS (mTLS)<br/>AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)"]
        AD["Active Directory<br/>AWS Directory Service"]
    end

    Endpoint -.->|Validate Identity| AuthenticationLayer

    subgraph AccessControl ["Access Control Engine"]
        AuthRules["Authorization Rules<br/>(Group-to-CIDR Mapping)"]
        SGs["Association Security Groups<br/>(Stateful Filtering)"]
    end

    Endpoint --> AccessControl

    subgraph TargetNetwork ["Target Network VPC"]
        AssocA["Subnet Association AZ-a<br/>(Managed ENI A)"]
        AssocB["Subnet Association AZ-b<br/>(Managed ENI B)"]
    end

    AccessControl --> TargetNetwork
    TargetNetwork --> Workloads["VPC Compute / RDS / Peered Networks"]

docs.title: 1. Client CIDR Range
docs.text:
• CIDR Block Size: Must be between a /22 (1,024 IP addresses) and /12 (1,048,576 IP addresses).
  • Non-Overlapping Requirement: The client CIDR block must not overlap with:
  • The VPC CIDR associated with the endpoint.
  • Any peered VPCs, Transit Gateway routes, or on-premises networks.
  • The local client network CIDR from which users connect (e.g. standard home Wi-Fi 192.168.1.0/24). A best practice is to assign 172.16.0.0/16 or 100.64.0.0/16 (CGNAT range).
  • Static Allocation: You cannot modify the client CIDR block after the endpoint is created.

docs.title: 2. Transport Protocol & Port Selection
docs.text:
AWS Client VPN supports ports 443 and 1194 for both UDP and TCP:

  • UDP Port 1194 (Default & Recommended): Delivers lowest latency and prevents TCP-over-TCP congestion collapse.
  • TCP Port 443: Best for users connecting from restrictive firewall environments where UDP traffic is blocked.

docs.title: 3. Split-Tunneling vs Full-Tunneling Configuration
docs.text:
• Split-Tunnel Enabled (Recommended): Only traffic destined for corporate subnets specified in the Client VPN route table is pushed through the tunnel. All standard internet traffic (web browsing, streaming) exits directly through the client's local internet gateway. This dramatically reduces AWS egress bandwidth charges and improves client connection speeds.
  • Split-Tunnel Disabled (Full Tunnel): A default route (0.0.0.0/0) is pushed to the client. All traffic—including public internet browsing—is routed into AWS and must egress through an AWS NAT Gateway or centralized firewall.

docs.title: 4. Custom DNS Servers & Route 53 Private Hosted Zones
docs.text:
You can configure up to two custom DNS server IP addresses on the endpoint:

  • In typical AWS deployments, specifying the Amazon-Provided DNS Server (the VPC router IP at Base VPC CIDR + 2, e.g. 10.0.0.2) allows connected clients to transparently resolve Amazon Route 53 Private Hosted Zones (such as api.internal.corp or db.internal.production).

docs.title: 5. Session Timeout & Maximum Connection Duration
docs.text:
• By default, Client VPN enforces a maximum connection duration of 24 hours. After 24 hours, the session terminates and requires the user to re-authenticate with the Identity Provider.
  • You can configure session timeout between 8, 10, 12, or 24 hours to align with internal enterprise security compliance policies.

docs.title: 6. Self-Service Portal
docs.text:
AWS Client VPN provides an optional AWS-hosted web portal where end users can log in using their corporate SSO credentials to download:

  1. The latest pre-configured OpenVPN configuration profile (.ovpn).
  2. The official AWS Client VPN desktop client application for macOS, Windows, or Linux.

This eliminates manual distribution of configuration files by cloud administrators.

docs.title: Architectural Constraints & Limits
docs.text: Constraint Limit Architectural Workaround / Best Practice Max Associated Subnets Unlimited subnets, but only 1 per AZ Associate across 2 or 3 AZs for multi-AZ high availability. VPC Tenancy Dedicated Tenancy is not supported Endpoint target VPC must use default (shared) tenancy. IPv6 Support IPv4 only Dual-stack workloads must be addressed via private IPv4. Max Routes per Endpoint Default limit: 50 routes Aggregate routes using CIDR summarization (e.g., 10.0.0.0/8 or 172.16.0.0/12).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A route table contains a set of rules (called routes) that determine where network packets from your subnet, gateway, or VPN endpoint are directed. In an AWS Client VPN architecture, routing occurs across two distinct layers:

  1. The Client VPN Endpoint Route Table: Controls which destination CIDR routes are pushed to connected VPN clients and permitted through the endpoint gateway.
  2. The Associated Subnet VPC Route Table: Dictates packet forwarding once traffic egresses the Client VPN Network Interface into the VPC.

docs.title: The Dual-Layer Routing Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Client["Connected Client<br/>Assigned IP: 172.16.0.5"] -->|Encrypted Tunnel| Endpoint["Client VPN Endpoint"]

    subgraph ClientVPNRouting ["Layer 1: Client VPN Route Table"]
        R1["Route 1: 10.0.0.0/16 to Associated Subnet"]
        R2["Route 2: 10.1.0.0/16 to Peered VPC"]
        R3["Route 3: 0.0.0.0/0 to Internet via NAT"]
    end

    Endpoint --> ClientVPNRouting
    ClientVPNRouting --> ENI["Subnet ENI<br/>SNAT IP: 10.0.10.15"]

    subgraph VPCRouting ["Layer 2: VPC Subnet Route Table"]
        VR1["10.0.0.0/16 to local"]
        VR2["10.1.0.0/16 to Peering Connection"]
        VR3["0.0.0.0/0 to NAT Gateway"]
    end

    ENI --> VPCRouting

The Two-Way Routing Requirement

For client traffic to reach a destination network (such as a peered VPC or an on-premises server):

  1. You must create a route in the Client VPN Endpoint Route Table targeting the destination CIDR.
  2. The VPC Route Table of the associated subnet must have a valid route targeting that same CIDR (e.g. via a Transit Gateway, Peering Connection, or Virtual Private Gateway).
  3. An Authorization Rule must exist on the Client VPN endpoint granting the client access to that CIDR.

docs.title: Route Priority: Longest Prefix Match (LPM)
docs.text:
AWS route tables follow the Longest Prefix Match algorithm. If multiple routes overlap, the most specific route (the one with the largest subnet mask / prefix length) takes precedence:

Destination CIDR Target Gateway Priority Context 10.0.0.0/16 local VPC-wide communication 10.0.1.0/24 eni-12345 Specific appliance override (more specific than /16) 0.0.0.0/0 nat-98765 Default catch-all route for outbound traffic

docs.title: Route Table Types in Enterprise AWS
1. Main Route Table
docs.text: The default route table automatically assigned to any subnet that is not explicitly associated with a custom route table. In production enterprise architectures, the main route table should be left empty or restricted to prevent accidental internet exposure of newly created subnets.

docs.title: 2. Custom Subnet Route Tables
docs.text:
Dedicated route tables associated explicitly with subnets:

  • Client VPN Association Route Table: Points local traffic to local, internet traffic (0.0.0.0/0) to an egress NAT Gateway, and corporate ranges to Transit Gateway (tgw-xxxx).
  • Private App Route Table: Isolated from public gateways.

docs.title: 3. Gateway & Edge Association Route Tables
docs.text: Associated directly with an Internet Gateway (IGW) or Virtual Private Gateway (VGW) to intercept inbound ingress traffic and route it through virtual firewall appliances (e.g., AWS Network Firewall or third-party NGFWs) before reaching workload subnets.

docs.title: Split-Tunnel vs Full-Tunnel Routing Table Behavior
docs.text: Parameter Split-Tunnel Enabled Full-Tunnel (Split-Tunnel Disabled) Default Route (0.0.0.0/0) Retained on client local ISP adapter Overwritten to point through Client VPN tunnel Corporate Routes Only specified CIDRs (e.g. 10.0.0.0/16) pushed to client OS All traffic pushed through Client VPN endpoint Bandwidth Cost Zero AWS egress cost for client web/streaming traffic High AWS egress cost; all web browsing traverses AWS NAT Gateway Enterprise Use Case Developer workstations & remote engineers High-security government or financial compliance environments requiring full internet inspection

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: An AWS Security Group acts as a distributed, stateful virtual firewall for Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs) attached to instances, containers, databases, and managed services. It evaluates traffic at the hypervisor layer, ensuring malicious packets are dropped before reaching the operating system.

docs.title: Stateful vs Stateless Inspection
docs.text:
Understanding the operational difference between Security Groups and Network ACLs (NACLs) is foundational to enterprise network security:

Feature AWS Security Group Network Access Control List (NACL) Operating Layer ENI / Instance Level Subnet Boundary Level State Tracking Stateful: Return traffic is automatically permitted regardless of inbound rules. Stateless: Inbound and outbound traffic must be explicitly permitted. Rule Processing Evaluates all rules across all attached security groups simultaneously before deciding to allow traffic. Evaluates numbered rules in sequential order (lowest number first) until a match occurs. Action Types Supports Allow rules only (implicit deny all). Supports both Allow and Deny rules.

docs.title: Security Group Chaining: The Enterprise Best Practice
docs.text:
In an AWS Client VPN deployment, administrators frequently make the mistake of allowing client IP CIDR ranges (e.g. 172.16.0.0/16) in workload security groups. This is an anti-pattern because Client VPN applies Source NAT (SNAT), and relying on IP ranges violates micro-segmentation principles.

The enterprise standard is Security Group Chaining (Referencing Security Group IDs):

flowchart LR
    subgraph ClientVPN ["AWS Client VPN Association"]
        VPN_ENI["Client VPN ENI"]
        SG_VPN["Client VPN Security Group<br/>(sg-vpn-access)"]
        VPN_ENI --- SG_VPN
    end

    subgraph AppTier ["Application Tier"]
        App_EC2["App EC2 / Container"]
        SG_APP["App Security Group<br/>(sg-app-workload)<br/>Ingress: TCP 443<br/>Source: sg-vpn-access"]
        App_EC2 --- SG_APP
    end

    subgraph DataTier ["Database Tier"]
        RDS_DB["Aurora / RDS Database"]
        SG_DB["Database Security Group<br/>(sg-database)<br/>Ingress: TCP 5432<br/>Source: sg-app-workload"]
        RDS_DB --- SG_DB
    end

    SG_VPN -->|Permitted via SG Reference| SG_APP
    SG_APP -->|Permitted via SG Reference| SG_DB
    SG_VPN -.->|Blocked: No Direct DB Access| SG_DB

docs.title: Why Security Group Chaining is Superior
docs.text:
1. Zero IP Dependency: Security group IDs are independent of IP allocations. If the Client CIDR or subnet CIDR changes, no firewall rules need to be updated.
  2. True Least Privilege: Only instances explicitly tagged with the authorized security group can initiate connections.
  3. Defense Against Lateral Movement: Even if an unauthorized client establishes a VPN session, they cannot connect directly to databases because the database security group permits connections only from the application security group (sg-app-workload).

docs.title: 1. Client VPN Association Security Group (sg-vpn-access)
docs.text:
Applied to the Client VPN target subnet association:

Direction Type Protocol Port Range Destination / Source Purpose Inbound None - - - Default deny; endpoints do not receive unsolicited inbound from VPC. Outbound HTTPS TCP 443 sg-app-workload Permitted outbound egress to application tier. Outbound SSH TCP 22 sg-bastion-mgmt Management access if explicitly needed.

docs.title: 2. Workload Application Security Group (sg-app-workload)
docs.text:
Applied to the application EC2 instances or EKS pods:

Direction Type Protocol Port Range Source Purpose Inbound HTTPS TCP 443 sg-vpn-access Allows VPN clients secure HTTPS management/web access. Outbound PostgreSQL TCP 5432 sg-database Forward queries to isolated database tier.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) provisions a logically isolated virtual network within the AWS Cloud. Designing an enterprise VPC requires careful IP address management (IPAM), multi-tier segmentation, and resilient routing topologies to support secure remote access via AWS Client VPN.

docs.title: Multi-Tier Subnet Topology
docs.text:
A robust VPC architecture segments network assets into functional tiers, enforcing least-privilege traffic flow between layers:

flowchart TD
    subgraph PublicSubnets ["Public Ingress Tier (DMZ)"]
        NAT1["NAT Gateway (AZ-a)"]
        NAT2["NAT Gateway (AZ-b)"]
        ALB["Application Load Balancer"]
    end

    subgraph VPNSubnets ["Client VPN Association Tier"]
        VPN_ENI1["Client VPN ENI (AZ-a)<br/>10.0.10.0/28"]
        VPN_ENI2["Client VPN ENI (AZ-b)<br/>10.0.11.0/28"]
    end

    subgraph PrivateAppSubnets ["Private Application Tier"]
        App1["EC2 / EKS Compute (AZ-a)"]
        App2["EC2 / EKS Compute (AZ-b)"]
    end

    subgraph IsolatedDataSubnets ["Isolated Database Tier"]
        RDS1["Aurora / RDS Primary (AZ-a)"]
        RDS2["Aurora / RDS Standby (AZ-b)"]
    end

    VPN_ENI1 --> App1
    VPN_ENI2 --> App2
    App1 --> RDS1
    App2 --> RDS2

docs.title: Subnet Tiers Breakdown
docs.text: Subnet Tier Routing Characteristics Workload Purpose Public Subnets Default route 0.0.0.0/0 targeting an Internet Gateway (IGW). NAT Gateways, Public ALBs. No backend compute. Client VPN Subnets Private subnets dedicated exclusively for Client VPN Endpoint associations. Managed ENIs provisioned by the Client VPN service. Private App Subnets Default route 0.0.0.0/0 targeting NAT Gateways for outbound internet updates. Microservices, EC2 instances, EKS worker nodes. Isolated Database Tier No route to internet gateways or NAT devices; strictly intra-VPC routing. RDS, DynamoDB VPC endpoints, Aurora clusters.

docs.title: CIDR Block Allocation (RFC 1918)
docs.text:
When planning a VPC that interfaces with AWS Client VPN, CIDR allocations must strictly avoid IP overlap:

  • VPC CIDR: Typically a /16 block (e.g. 10.0.0.0/16 providing 65,536 addresses).
  • Client VPN Client CIDR: Must not overlap with the VPC CIDR, any peered VPCs, or corporate on-premises subnets (e.g., allocating 172.16.0.0/16 or 10.100.0.0/16 specifically for connecting clients).
  • Minimum Subnet Size: Target subnets associated with Client VPN require at least a /27 or /28 mask to accommodate AWS reserved IPs and managed ENIs.

AWS Reserved IP Addresses in Every Subnet

In every AWS subnet, the first four and last IP addresses are reserved by AWS:

  • 10.0.0.0: Network address.
  • 10.0.0.1: Reserved by AWS for the VPC router.
  • 10.0.0.2: Reserved by AWS for DNS (AmazonProvidedDNS).
  • 10.0.0.3: Reserved by AWS for future use.
  • 10.0.0.255: Network broadcast address (broadcast is not supported in VPC).

docs.title: VPC Endpoints & PrivateLink
docs.text:
VPC Endpoints allow instances and VPN clients to privately communicate with supported AWS services (e.g., S3, CloudWatch Logs, Systems Manager) without traversing the public internet.

  • Gateway Endpoints: Cost-free route table entries directing S3 and DynamoDB traffic privately over the AWS backbone.
  • Interface Endpoints (PrivateLink): Elastic Network Interfaces with private IP addresses serving as entry points for AWS services (e.g., ec2.us-east-1.amazonaws.com or CloudWatch Logs logs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com).
  • Client VPN Relevance: When Client VPN users are connected, they can resolve and interact with PrivateLink endpoints directly over the VPN tunnel, keeping administrative traffic off the public internet.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Securing remote ingress requires separating Authentication (validating user identity and device integrity) from Authorization (enforcing least-privilege access to specific destination networks). AWS Client VPN supports enterprise identity federation coupled with granular, group-based authorization rules.

docs.title: Authentication Mechanisms
docs.text:
AWS Client VPN supports three enterprise-grade authentication models:

flowchart TD
    Client["Connecting Client"] --> AuthDecision{"Select Authentication Type"}

    AuthDecision -->|Enterprise Standard| SAML["1. Federated SAML 2.0<br/>(Okta / Entra ID / IAM Identity Center)<br/>Web-based MFA and Conditional Access"]
    AuthDecision -->|Certificate-Based| mTLS["2. Mutual TLS (mTLS)<br/>AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)<br/>Device and Server Certificates"]
    AuthDecision -->|Directory Service| AD["3. Active Directory<br/>AWS Directory Service<br/>Domain Credentials"]

docs.title: 1. Federated Authentication via SAML 2.0 (Recommended)
docs.text: SAML 2.0 federation is the gold standard for enterprise Zero-Trust architectures. It delegates authentication to an enterprise Identity Provider (IdP) such as Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD), Okta, or AWS IAM Identity Center.

docs.title: Key Benefits
docs.text:
• Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): Users complete hardware token, FIDO2/WebAuthn, or push notification MFA before establishing the VPN tunnel.
  • Conditional Access Policies: Enforce device compliance, corporate-managed device checks, and geofencing prior to allowing connections.
  • Single Sign-On (SSO): Eliminates separate VPN passwords; engineers authenticate using their corporate single sign-on credentials.
  • Automated Offboarding: Deactivating an employee in the corporate IdP immediately revokes their ability to authenticate with Client VPN.

docs.title: SAML Integration Flow
docs.text:
1. An IAM SAML Identity Provider is created in AWS containing the IdP's metadata XML.
  2. A dedicated Client VPN IAM application is registered within the enterprise IdP (e.g., Okta application or Entra Enterprise Application).
  3. The IdP is configured to return the user's Active Directory / IdP Groups attribute in the SAML assertion.
  4. AWS Client VPN inspects these group assertions to enforce granular network authorization rules.

docs.title: 2. Mutual Authentication (mTLS)
docs.text:
Mutual authentication utilizes X.509 digital certificates to authenticate both the client device and the AWS Client VPN server.

  • Server Certificate: Provisioned and stored in AWS Certificate Manager (ACM). Verifies the authenticity of the VPN endpoint to connecting clients.
  • Client Certificate: Installed on the client workstation.
  • Certificate Revocation Lists (CRL): If a client certificate is lost or an employee departs, administrators generate a CRL and upload it to the Client VPN endpoint to block compromised certificates.

docs.title: 3. Active Directory Authentication
docs.text:
Enables authentication against an Active Directory domain via AWS Directory Service (AWS Managed Microsoft AD, Simple AD, or AD Connector pointing to an on-premises domain controller).

  • Users authenticate using their standard domain username and password.
  • Supports Active Directory group queries for network authorization.

docs.title: Network-Based Authorization Rules
docs.text:
AWS Client VPN operates on a strict Default Deny security posture. Even after a client successfully authenticates, they cannot send packets to any subnet or IP address until an explicit Authorization Rule is configured.

flowchart TD
    subgraph ClientVPN ["Client VPN Endpoint"]
        ClientUser["User: alice@corp.com<br/>Groups: CloudEng, SRE"]
    end

    subgraph AuthRules ["Authorization Rules Engine"]
        Rule1["Rule A: Group CloudEng<br/>Permitted: 10.0.0.0/16"]
        Rule2["Rule B: Group ProdAdmins<br/>Permitted: 10.10.0.0/16"]
        Rule3["Rule C: All Clients<br/>Permitted: 10.0.100.0/24"]
    end

    ClientUser --> Rule1
    ClientUser --> Rule2
    ClientUser --> Rule3

    Rule1 -->|MATCH: ALLOW| TargetA["VPC Core (10.0.0.0/16)"]
    Rule2 -.->|NO MATCH: DENY| TargetB["Prod Workloads (10.10.0.0/16)"]
    Rule3 -->|MATCH: ALLOW| TargetC["Internal Wiki (10.0.100.0/24)"]

docs.title: Authorization Rule Structure
docs.text:
Each authorization rule specifies three parameters:

Field Configuration Options Description Destination Network CIDR e.g. 10.0.1.0/24, 10.0.0.0/16, 0.0.0.0/0 The specific network block the rule permits access to. Grant Access To Specific Active Directory / SAML Group ID OR All Clients (*) The exact group allowed to traverse the tunnel to this destination CIDR. Description String Operational documentation explaining the business justification.

docs.title: Enterprise Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) Matrix
docs.text: Identity Group Destination CIDR Target Resources Access Rationale devops-engineers 10.0.0.0/16 All Development & Staging VPC subnets Infrastructure provisioning and deployment debugging. data-analysts 10.0.50.0/24 Read-only analytics RDS & Redshift clusters Query execution without access to compute tiers. all-employees 10.0.200.0/24 Corporate Intranet & Jira private instances General internal productivity tools. contractors 10.0.10.45/32 Specific isolated test environment host Zero lateral movement allowed.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Comprehensive observability across remote ingress is mandatory for compliance (SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI-DSS), capacity planning, and incident response. AWS Client VPN provides telemetry across three complementary layers:

flowchart TD
    Endpoint["AWS Client VPN Endpoint"] --> Stream1["1. Amazon CloudWatch Metrics<br/>Real-time aggregation: ActiveConnections, BytesIn, BytesOut"]
    Endpoint --> Stream2["2. CloudWatch Connection Logs<br/>Session audit trail: IPs, common names, start and end timestamps"]
    Endpoint --> Stream3["3. VPC Flow Logs on Subnet ENIs<br/>Packet-level L4 metadata: Src, Dst, Port, Action"]
    Endpoint --> Stream4["4. AWS CloudTrail<br/>Administrative API audits: Endpoint creation, route modification"]

docs.title: 1. Amazon CloudWatch Metrics
docs.text:
AWS Client VPN publishes quantitative operational metrics to CloudWatch in 5-minute increments under the AWS/ClientVPN namespace:

Metric Name Unit Architectural Significance ActiveConnections Count Number of concurrently active client sessions. Used for capacity planning and detecting connection anomalies. IngressBytes Bytes Data volume sent from clients to the Client VPN endpoint. Identifies heavy upload or bulk data transfers. EgressBytes Bytes Data volume forwarded from the endpoint back to clients. Monitors database query dumps or large artifact downloads. IngressPackets Count Total packet count ingress into the endpoint. Useful for packet-per-second (PPS) threshold monitoring. EgressPackets Count Total packet count egress back to client workstations.

docs.title: Alarm 1: Sudden Active Connection Surge (Credential Compromise Indicator)
docs.text:
• Namespace: AWS/ClientVPN
  • Metric: ActiveConnections
  • Statistic: Maximum
  • Threshold: > 150% of standard baseline
  • Period: 5 minutes
  • Action: Trigger AWS SNS notification to SecOps Slack channel.

docs.title: Alarm 2: Abnormal Ingress/Egress Bandwidth Spike (Data Exfiltration Indicator)
docs.text:
• Metric: EgressBytes
  • Statistic: Sum
  • Threshold: > 25 GB in 15 minutes
  • Action: Flag for immediate DLP (Data Loss Prevention) review.

docs.title: 2. CloudWatch Connection Logging
docs.text:
When Connection Logging is enabled, the endpoint streams real-time JSON log entries for every connection attempt, establishment, reset, and termination:

{
    "connection-log-type": "connection-attempt",
    "connection-attempt-status": "successful",
    "connection-reset-status": "NA",
    "connection-attempt-failure-reason": "NA",
    "connection-id": "cvpn-connection-0123456789abcdef0",
    "client-vpn-endpoint-id": "cvpn-endpoint-0123456789abcdef0",
    "transport-protocol": "udp",
    "connection-start-time": "2026-10-24 14:30:15",
    "connection-last-update-time": "2026-10-24 14:30:15",
    "client-ip": "172.16.0.45",
    "common-name": "alice.developer@mycorp.com",
    "device-type": "mac",
    "device-ip": "198.51.100.24",
    "port": "51240",
    "ingress-bytes": "1428500",
    "egress-bytes": "8942100",
    "ingress-packets": "1240",
    "egress-packets": "6850",
    "connection-end-time": "2026-10-24 18:45:00"
}

docs.title: Key Forensic Fields Explained
docs.text:
• common-name: The authenticated username (from SAML assertion or certificate CN).
  • device-ip: The public IP address of the user's home or remote internet connection.
  • client-ip: The private IPv4 address assigned to the client from the VPN Client CIDR block.
  • ingress-bytes / egress-bytes: Total bandwidth consumed during the session.

docs.title: CloudWatch Logs Insights Forensic Queries
docs.text: Security teams can run these structured queries in Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights against the Client VPN log group:

docs.title: Query 1: Top 10 Remote Users by Data Volume Transferred
docs.text:
fields @timestamp, `common-name`, `device-ip`, (`ingress-bytes` + `egress-bytes`) / 1048576 as TotalMB
| filter `connection-attempt-status` = "successful"
| stats sum(TotalMB) as TotalBandwidthMB by `common-name`
| sort TotalBandwidthMB desc
| limit 10

docs.title: Query 2: Failed Connection Attempts & Failure Reasons
docs.text:
fields @timestamp, `common-name`, `device-ip`, `connection-attempt-failure-reason`
| filter `connection-attempt-status` = "failed"
| stats count(*) as FailureCount by `common-name`, `device-ip`, `connection-attempt-failure-reason`
| sort FailureCount desc

docs.title: Query 3: Active Sessions Exceeding 8 Hours
docs.text:
fields @timestamp, `common-name`, `device-ip`, `connection-id`
| filter `connection-attempt-status` = "successful" and isempty(`connection-end-time`)
| sort @timestamp asc

docs.title: 3. Correlating Client VPN with VPC Flow Logs
docs.text:
Because Client VPN applies Source NAT (SNAT), target instances see traffic originating from the Subnet ENI's IP address (e.g. 10.0.10.12).

flowchart LR
    Log1["CloudWatch Connection Log<br/>User: alice<br/>Client IP: 172.16.0.45<br/>Time: 14:30:15"] 
    Log2["VPC Flow Log (Subnet ENI)<br/>Src: 10.0.10.12<br/>Dst: 10.0.1.50 (RDS)<br/>Port: 5432<br/>Time: 14:30:16"]

    Log1 -.->|Correlate via Timestamp and Active Window| IncidentReport["Unified Forensic Audit Trail<br/>Proof of User Query to RDS"]
    Log2 -.-> IncidentReport

To reconstruct an incident: 1. Identify the internal target host and timestamp from application or database logs. 2. Search VPC Flow Logs for connections originating from the Client VPN Subnet ENI to that host. 3. Query Client VPN Connection Logs for active sessions during that exact timestamp to identify the specific engineer (common-name) and remote public IP (device-ip).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Securing an enterprise remote access gateway requires a Defense-in-Depth model spanning cryptographic cipher enforcement, identity governance, endpoint posture validation, session lifecycle controls, and strict IAM administrative boundaries.

docs.title: Defense-in-Depth Security Layers
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    Layer1["1. Cryptographic Security<br/>TLS 1.2 / 1.3 - AES-256-GCM - SHA-384"] --> Layer2
    Layer2["2. Identity and Access Governance<br/>SAML 2.0 MFA - SSO - Dynamic Revocation"] --> Layer3
    Layer3["3. Network Segmentation<br/>Group-based Auth Rules - Default Deny"] --> Layer4
    Layer4["4. Stateful Virtual Firewalling<br/>Security Group Chaining - ENI SNAT"] --> Layer5
    Layer5["5. Observability and Forensic Audit<br/>CloudWatch Logs - VPC Flow Logs - Alarms"]

docs.title: Cryptographic Hardening & TLS Configuration
docs.text:
AWS Client VPN establishes encrypted tunnels using Transport Layer Security (TLS). To adhere to modern cybersecurity standards (such as NIST SP 800-52 and CIS AWS Benchmarks):

  1. Protocol Standards: Enforce TLS 1.2 minimum on all endpoint associations.
  2. Cipher Suites: AWS Client VPN negotiates industry-standard authenticated encryption ciphers:
  3. ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384
  4. ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256
  5. DHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384
  6. Transport Security: Avoid using self-signed root certificates in production. Always utilize private or public Certificate Authorities registered within AWS Certificate Manager (ACM).

docs.title: Certificate Revocation & Emergency Offboarding
docs.text: When an employee departs or a laptop is reported lost or compromised, administrators must immediately revoke network access.

docs.title: 1. Generating and Applying a Certificate Revocation List (CRL)
docs.text:
Using OpenSSL or EasyRSA, administrators generate a CRL and import it to the endpoint:

# Generate the updated CRL file
openssl ca -gencrl -out crl.pem -config openssl.cnf

# Import the CRL into AWS Client VPN
aws ec2 import-client-vpn-client-certificate-revocation-list \
    --client-vpn-endpoint-id cvpn-endpoint-0123456789abcdef0 \
    --certificate-revocation-list file://crl.pem \
    --region us-east-1

Once imported, AWS Client VPN immediately drops any existing sessions utilizing the revoked certificate and blocks future handshake attempts.

docs.title: 2. Immediate Session Termination
docs.text:
To forcefully disconnect an active suspicious session without waiting for session expiration:

# Terminate a specific compromised connection
aws ec2 terminate-client-vpn-connections \
    --client-vpn-endpoint-id cvpn-endpoint-0123456789abcdef0 \
    --connection-id cvpn-connection-0123456789abcdef0 \
    --region us-east-1

docs.title: Client Connect Handler: Device Posture Assessment
docs.text:
For enterprise environments requiring Zero-Trust endpoint posture assessment, AWS Client VPN supports Client Connect Handlers:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Client as Remote Client
    participant Endpoint as Client VPN Endpoint
    participant Lambda as Validation Lambda
    participant EDR as Enterprise EDR [CrowdStrike]

    Client->>Endpoint: Submit connection request
    Endpoint->>Lambda: Trigger Connect Handler with device metadata
    Lambda->>EDR: Query device compliance status
    alt Device Compliant
        EDR-->>Lambda: Compliant (Status Green)
        Lambda-->>Endpoint: Return Allow
        Endpoint-->>Client: Establish VPN Session
    else Device Non-Compliant
        EDR-->>Lambda: Non-Compliant (Status Red)
        Lambda-->>Endpoint: Return Deny
        Endpoint-->>Client: Reject Connection and Log Alert
    end

docs.title: Least-Privilege IAM Administrative Policies
docs.text: Administrative access to configure and modify AWS Client VPN resources must be restricted using Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) and least-privilege IAM policies.

docs.title: 1. Read-Only Auditor Policy
docs.text:
Grants security auditors visibility into routes, endpoints, and active connections without modification rights:

{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Sid": "ClientVPNAuditorReadOnly",
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": [
                "ec2:DescribeClientVpnEndpoints",
                "ec2:DescribeClientVpnTargetNetworks",
                "ec2:DescribeClientVpnConnections",
                "ec2:DescribeClientVpnRoutes",
                "ec2:DescribeClientVpnAuthorizationRules"
            ],
            "Resource": "*"
        }
    ]
}

docs.title: 2. Scoped Administrator Policy with ABAC Tag Enforcement
docs.text:
Restricts network engineers to managing only endpoints tagged with Environment = NonProduction:

{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Sid": "ManageTaggedClientVPNOnly",
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": [
                "ec2:AssociateClientVpnTargetNetwork",
                "ec2:DisassociateClientVpnTargetNetwork",
                "ec2:ApplySecurityGroupsToClientVpnTargetNetwork",
                "ec2:AuthorizeClientVpnIngress",
                "ec2:RevokeClientVpnIngress",
                "ec2:CreateClientVpnRoute",
                "ec2:DeleteClientVpnRoute"
            ],
            "Resource": "arn:aws:ec2:*:*:client-vpn-endpoint/*",
            "Condition": {
                "StringEquals": {
                    "aws:ResourceTag/Environment": "NonProduction"
                }
            }
        }
    ]
}

docs.title: Threat Modeling & Mitigation Matrix
docs.text: Threat Vector Potential Impact Architecture Mitigation Credential Phishing Unauthorized VPN ingress Mandatory SAML 2.0 with FIDO2 / Hardware MFA; session timeout capped at 10 hours. Stolen Workstation Lateral movement into cloud subnets Device Posture Check Lambda, Certificate Revocation Lists (CRL), Security Group Chaining. Rogue Route Injection Traffic redirection to malicious IP IAM ABAC policies restricting ec2:CreateClientVpnRoute to approved CI/CD pipelines. Overlapping IP Collisions Routing failures or blackholed traffic Strict RFC 1918 CIDR reservation policy; client pool assigned to non-standard block (100.64.0.0/16).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
AWS Client VPN scales across diverse enterprise topologies—from single development VPCs to complex multi-account hub-and-spoke networks connected via AWS Transit Gateway and on-premises datacenters.

This chapter details the five essential enterprise architecture patterns, complete with routing matrices, authorization rules, and security controls.

docs.title: Scenario 1: Secure Access to a Single VPC Workload Tier
docs.text: The foundational deployment pattern provides remote engineers direct, encrypted access to workloads in a single private VPC without exposing public bastion jump hosts.

docs.title: Architecture Highlights
docs.text:
• Endpoint Association: Associated with private subnets across two Availability Zones (us-east-1a and us-east-1b) for high availability.
  • Split Tunnel: Enabled. Only packets destined for the VPC CIDR (10.0.0.0/16) route through the VPN tunnel.
  • DNS Resolution: The AmazonProvidedDNS (10.0.0.2) resolves Route 53 Private Hosted Zones (*.internal.mycorp).

docs.title: Configuration Matrix
docs.text: Layer Configuration Item Value Client VPN Route Table Destination CIDR 10.0.0.0/16 targeting Associated Subnet Client VPN Authorization Destination CIDR 10.0.0.0/16 granted to EngineeringGroup VPC Route Table Local Route 10.0.0.0/16 to local Workload Security Group Inbound HTTPS / SSH Ingress allowed from sg-client-vpn (Security Group Chaining)

docs.title: Scenario 2: Multi-VPC Access via VPC Peering & Transit Gateway
docs.text: Enterprises managing multi-account AWS environments often establish a central Shared Services / Ingress VPC housing the Client VPN endpoint, granting access to workloads in peered Production and Staging VPCs.

docs.title: The Routing Requirement
docs.text:
AWS VPC Peering does not support edge-to-edge transitive routing by default. To route client traffic through the Associated Subnet to a peered VPC (10.1.0.0/16):

  1. The Client VPN Endpoint Route Table must have an explicit route for 10.1.0.0/16.
  2. The VPC Route Table of the associated subnet must route 10.1.0.0/16 to the Peering Connection ID (pcx-xxxx) or Transit Gateway (tgw-xxxx).
  3. An Authorization Rule must grant clients permission to 10.1.0.0/16.

docs.title: Configuration Matrix
docs.text: Route Table Destination CIDR Target Gateway Purpose Client VPN Route Table 10.0.0.0/16 Associated Subnet Local Ingress VPC routing Client VPN Route Table 10.1.0.0/16 Associated Subnet Peered Workload VPC routing Associated Subnet VPC RT 10.1.0.0/16 pcx-0123456789abcdef0 Forwards traffic across VPC peer Peered Subnet VPC RT 10.0.0.0/16 pcx-0123456789abcdef0 Returns traffic back to Ingress VPC ENI

docs.title: Scenario 3: Hybrid Cloud Connectivity (On-Premises Data Center)
docs.text: Remote engineers frequently require simultaneous access to both AWS cloud workloads and legacy on-premises datacenters over a single VPN connection.

docs.title: Architecture Highlights
docs.text:
• The Ingress VPC is connected to the on-premises datacenter via an AWS Direct Connect (DX) private virtual interface or an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection terminating on a Virtual Private Gateway (VGW) or Transit Gateway (TGW).
  • Client traffic destined for 192.168.0.0/16 (on-prem) enters the Client VPN endpoint, undergoes SNAT at the Subnet ENI, and forwards across the Direct Connect / Site-to-Site tunnel.

docs.title: Configuration Matrix
docs.text: Route Layer Destination CIDR Target Gateway Notes Client VPN Route 192.168.0.0/16 Associated Subnet Directs on-premises traffic to the association VPC Route Table 192.168.0.0/16 vgw-0123456789 or tgw-0123456789 Traverses hybrid cloud link On-Premises Firewall 10.0.10.0/28 (VPN Subnet) Inbound DX Gateway Must allow return traffic to the VPN subnet ENI

docs.title: Scenario 4: Secure Internet Egress via Centralized NAT Gateway / Firewall
docs.text: In strict compliance environments (financial services, healthcare), organizations mandate that all remote client internet traffic be inspected, logged, and filtered through centralized egress inspection proxies or the AWS Network Firewall.

docs.title: Architecture Highlights
docs.text:
• Split Tunneling is Disabled: Forces all client traffic (0.0.0.0/0) into the Client VPN tunnel.
  • Traffic egresses the Client VPN ENI into a private subnet, whose route table points 0.0.0.0/0 to an AWS NAT Gateway in a public subnet.
  • Public web servers receive traffic originating from the Elastic IP of the NAT Gateway, masking user home IPs and enabling IP-whitelisting on third-party SaaS platforms.

docs.title: Configuration Matrix
docs.text: Component Setting Value Client VPN Endpoint Split Tunnel Disabled (Full Tunnel Mode) Client VPN Route Table Destination 0.0.0.0/0 targeting Associated Subnet Authorization Rule Destination 0.0.0.0/0 granted to all clients or specific groups Associated Subnet Route Table 0.0.0.0/0 Targets NAT Gateway (nat-0123456789)

docs.title: Scenario 5: Group-Based Micro-Segmentation (Dev vs. Prod)
docs.text:
A single Client VPN endpoint can securely serve multiple departments with strict micro-segmentation, eliminating the cost of running separate endpoints for dev, staging, and prod:

flowchart LR
    DevUser["Developer<br/>(Group: DevTeam)"] --> Endpoint["Client VPN Endpoint<br/>(Single Shared Endpoint)"]
    AdminUser["Security Admin<br/>(Group: SecAdmins)"] --> Endpoint

    Endpoint --> RuleDev{"Auth Rule: DevTeam"}
    Endpoint --> RuleProd{"Auth Rule: SecAdmins"}

    RuleDev -->|ALLOWED| DevVPC["Development VPC Subnet<br/>(10.0.1.0/24)"]
    RuleDev -.->|BLOCKED| ProdVPC["Production VPC Subnet<br/>(10.0.2.0/24)"]

    RuleProd -->|ALLOWED| DevVPC
    RuleProd -->|ALLOWED| ProdVPC

docs.title: Authorization Rules Matrix
docs.text:
1. Rule 1: Destination 10.0.1.0/24 to Authorized Group: DevTeam
  2. Rule 2: Destination 10.0.2.0/24 to Authorized Group: SecAdmins
  3. Rule 3: Destination 10.0.200.0/24 (Corporate Docs) to Authorized Group: * (All Users)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Understanding the exact end-to-end packet flow and session handshake lifecycle of AWS Client VPN is essential for network troubleshooting, latency optimization, and security forensics.

docs.title: The End-to-End Session Handshake & Packet Lifecycle
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor User as Remote Client
    participant DNS as Route 53 Public DNS
    participant Endpoint as Client VPN Endpoint
    participant IdP as Identity Provider [SAML/Okta]
    participant ENI as Target Subnet ENI [SNAT]
    participant Target as Target EC2 / RDS Instance

    Note over User,Endpoint: Phase 1: Connection & Authentication
    User->>DNS: Resolve *.cvpn-endpoint-xxxx.amazonaws.com
    DNS-->>User: Returns randomized AWS Endpoint IP
    User->>Endpoint: Initiate TLS Handshake (UDP 1194 / TCP 443)
    Endpoint-->>User: Request Credentials / SAML Assertion
    User->>IdP: Authenticate with Corporate SSO & MFA
    IdP-->>User: Issue Signed SAML Response Token
    User->>Endpoint: Submit SAML Assertion
    Endpoint->>Endpoint: Validate Token Signature & Group Membership

    Note over User,Endpoint: Phase 2: Tunnel Configuration
    Endpoint-->>User: Assign Client IP (e.g. 172.16.0.45 from CIDR Pool)
    Endpoint-->>User: Push Routing Table Entries & DNS Servers
    User->>User: Configure Virtual TUN Adapter & Inject OS Routes

    Note over User,Target: Phase 3: Active Data Transfer
    User->>User: Application initiates TCP request to 10.0.1.50
    User->>Endpoint: Encapsulated & Encrypted Packet (Outer UDP 1194)
    Endpoint->>Endpoint: Decrypt TLS & Verify Authorization Rule
    Endpoint->>ENI: Forward to Associated Subnet ENI
    Note over ENI: Perform Source NAT (SNAT: 172.16.0.45 to 10.0.10.12)
    ENI->>Target: Egress Packet to VPC Subnet (Src: 10.0.10.12, Dst: 10.0.1.50)
    Target-->>ENI: Send Response Packet
    ENI-->>Endpoint: Reverse NAT
    Endpoint-->>User: Encapsulate & Return to Client over VPN Tunnel

docs.title: Phase 1: DNS Resolution & Endpoint Randomization
docs.text:
1. The OpenVPN configuration file (.ovpn) contains an endpoint DNS name prefixed with an asterisk: *.cvpn-endpoint-0123456789abcdef0.prod.clientvpn.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
  2. When the client establishes a connection, the client software prepends a random alphanumeric string (e.g., asdf123.cvpn-endpoint-...).
  3. This triggers a unique DNS query to Amazon Route 53, preventing DNS caching and automatically distributing incoming client sessions across AWS's underlying high-availability endpoint fleet.

docs.title: Phase 2: TLS Handshake & Authentication Verification
docs.text:
1. The client establishes a TLS 1.2 or 1.3 session with the Client VPN endpoint over UDP port 1194 or TCP port 443.
  2. If Federated SAML Authentication is configured:
  3. A local web browser opens automatically on the client machine to complete SSO authentication and MFA with the enterprise IdP (e.g. Okta, Azure AD, Ping Identity).
  4. The IdP issues a signed SAML response containing the user's identity and group attributes.
  5. The AWS Client VPN endpoint verifies the SAML token against the configured IAM SAML Identity Provider.
  6. If Mutual TLS (mTLS) is used:
  7. The endpoint verifies the client's x509 certificate against the Certificate Authority (CA) imported into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM).

docs.title: Phase 3: Address Leasing & Route Injection
docs.text:
1. The endpoint leases a unique private IPv4 address from the configured Client CIDR range (e.g., 172.16.0.45 from 172.16.0.0/16).
  2. The endpoint sends configuration parameters back to the client software:
  3. Client IP & Subnet Mask
  4. Route Table Entries (e.g., 10.0.0.0/16 for VPC, 10.1.0.0/16 for Peered VPC)
  5. DNS Servers (e.g., 10.0.0.2 Amazon-Provided DNS)
  6. The client OS injects these routes into its local kernel routing table, binding them to the virtual TUN network adapter.

docs.title: Phase 4: Encapsulation, Egress & Source NAT (SNAT)
docs.text:
1. When an engineer connects to a private internal resource (such as 10.0.1.50:5432), the client kernel intercepts the packet via the TUN adapter.
  2. The payload is encrypted with AES-256-GCM and encapsulated inside an outer UDP or TCP packet destined for the AWS Client VPN endpoint.
  3. Upon receipt, the AWS Client VPN endpoint:
  4. Decrypts the outer packet.
  5. Checks the Authorization Rules to confirm whether the user's group is permitted to access 10.0.1.50/32.
  6. Checks the Endpoint Route Table to locate the target network association.
  7. The packet is sent to the Elastic Network Interface (ENI) in the associated subnet.
  8. The ENI performs Source NAT (SNAT), rewriting the source IP address from 172.16.0.45 to the ENI's private IP (10.0.10.12).
  9. The packet traverses the VPC switching fabric, adheres to VPC route tables, passes through destination Security Groups, and reaches the target instance.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: An Elastic Network Interface (ENI) is a logical networking component in an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) that represents a virtual network interface card (vNIC). It provides IP addressing, MAC addressing, security group attachment, and network traffic control.

docs.title: The AWS Client VPN Managed ENI
docs.text:
When you associate a subnet with an AWS Client VPN endpoint, AWS automatically provisions and manages an Elastic Network Interface within that target subnet on your behalf.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Client as Remote Engineer [172.16.0.45]
    participant Endpoint as Client VPN Endpoint
    participant ENI as Subnet ENI [10.0.10.12]
    participant App as Target EC2 [10.0.1.50]

    Client->>Endpoint: Send HTTP Request (Src: 172.16.0.45, Dst: 10.0.1.50)
    Note over Endpoint,ENI: Decapsulation and Source NAT (SNAT)
    Endpoint->>ENI: Forward packet to target subnet
    ENI->>App: Egress packet (Src: 10.0.10.12, Dst: 10.0.1.50)
    Note over App: App logs observe traffic from 10.0.10.12
    App-->>ENI: Send Response (Src: 10.0.1.50, Dst: 10.0.10.12)
    ENI-->>Endpoint: Reverse NAT translation
    Endpoint-->>Client: Encapsulate and return to Client

docs.title: Critical Architectural Implications of Client VPN ENIs
1. Source Network Address Translation (SNAT)
docs.text:
As demonstrated above, traffic exiting the Client VPN endpoint into your VPC undergoes Source NAT (SNAT):

  • The source IP address from the client CIDR pool (172.16.0.0/16) is translated to the private IP address of the Client VPN network interface in the associated subnet.
  • Security & Firewall Impact: Workload instances (web servers, databases) will never receive packets with the client's original 172.16.x.x address. They only observe traffic originating from the Subnet ENI's IP address (10.0.10.12).
  • Forensic Audit Consequence: Application access logs (such as Nginx or PostgreSQL logs) will show all client requests originating from the same ENI IP address. To audit which individual developer initiated a specific connection, security teams must correlate application timestamps with AWS Client VPN Connection Logs in CloudWatch Logs.

docs.title: 2. ENI Provisioning & Lifecycle
docs.text:
• Automatic Scaling: As concurrent VPN connections scale up, AWS manages the underlying throughput capacity of the endpoint network interfaces.
  • Security Group Binding: You can associate up to 5 security groups directly with the Client VPN target network association. These security groups govern all traffic egressing from the managed ENIs.
  • Immutability: You cannot detach, modify, or delete the managed Client VPN ENI directly from the EC2 console. The ENI is automatically decommissioned only when the subnet association is disassociated via the Client VPN management API.

docs.title: Enterprise Use Cases for Multiple Network Interfaces (Dual-Homing)
docs.text:
Beyond Client VPN endpoints, standard EC2 compute workloads frequently utilize multiple ENIs for network isolation:

Architecture Pattern Description Security Benefit Management Network Isolation Primary ENI (eth0) handles public application traffic; secondary ENI (eth1) connects to a private management subnet accessible only via Client VPN. Isolates SSH/management traffic from external public data flows. Dual-Homed Security Appliances Virtual firewall appliances (e.g. pfSense, Palo Alto VM-Series) with an untrusted interface in a public subnet and a trusted interface in a private subnet. Enables stateful inline packet inspection before traffic enters internal VPC subnets. Distinct Subnet Workload Roles An instance simultaneously connected to a frontend web subnet and an isolated backend messaging subnet. Enforces micro-segmentation without routing through intermediate routers.

docs.title: Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
docs.text:
An architectural and operational reference addressing common design decisions, performance tradeoffs, and security controls for AWS Client VPN.

1. Why choose AWS Client VPN over self-managed OpenVPN Access Server on EC2?

While running OpenVPN Access Server on an EC2 instance may appear cheaper initially, it introduces significant hidden operational liabilities and security risks:

  • High Availability & Failover: An EC2 instance is a single point of failure. Setting up active/active clustering across Availability Zones with elastic IPs and state synchronization requires complex custom scripting and maintenance.
  • Maintenance & Patching: Operating system patches, OpenSSL zero-day vulnerability remediations, and Linux kernel updates must be maintained and audited manually.
  • Throughput Bottlenecks: Scaling an EC2 instance requires resizing instance types, which terminates active connections. AWS Client VPN elastically provisions capacity behind the scenes.
  • Native AWS Integration: AWS Client VPN integrates natively with AWS Certificate Manager, Amazon CloudWatch Logs, IAM SAML federation, and AWS Directory Service without third-party plugins.
2. What is the business and cost impact of Split-Tunneling?

Enabling Split-Tunneling is a recommended cloud best practice for general engineering access:

  • Bandwidth Cost Reduction: Without split-tunneling (Full-Tunnel mode), high-bandwidth client traffic (Zoom video calls, YouTube, personal downloads) routes into AWS and egresses through AWS NAT Gateways, incurring substantial NAT data processing and internet egress fees ($0.045/GB + $0.09/GB).
  • Latency Optimization: Direct internet traffic exits through the user's home ISP connection, providing faster speeds and avoiding double-hop latency to AWS data centers.
  • Battery & Performance: Reduces local CPU encryption overhead on client laptops by only encrypting traffic bound for corporate IP subnets.
3. Should we configure UDP port 1194 or TCP port 443?

UDP port 1194 is strongly recommended for production workloads.

  • Preventing TCP-over-TCP Meltdown: Running TCP inside TCP (such as web browsing or SSH over a TCP-based VPN tunnel) creates the TCP meltdown phenomenon: packet drops cause both inner and outer layers to initiate independent retransmissions and exponential backoffs, causing throughput to collapse.
  • Fallback Profile: TCP port 443 should only be provided as a secondary fallback profile for engineers connecting from restrictive hotel, airport, or client guest Wi-Fi networks that block outbound UDP traffic.
4. How do connected clients resolve private internal domain names?

Configure the DNS Servers parameter on the Client VPN endpoint to point to the Amazon-Provided DNS server (VPC Base IP + 2, e.g. 10.0.0.2).

  • When connected, the client's DNS queries for Route 53 Private Hosted Zones (e.g. api.internal.mycorp or db.staging.aws) are resolved privately through the VPC DNS resolver without leaking internal domain records to public DNS resolvers.
  • For split-tunnel configurations, public DNS queries continue resolving via the client's local DNS servers.
5. Can a single Client VPN endpoint grant access to multiple VPCs?

Yes. While a Client VPN endpoint can only be associated with subnets in a single VPC (the Ingress VPC), clients can reach workloads in any number of adjacent VPCs if you:

  1. Establish VPC Peering or connect the Ingress VPC to an AWS Transit Gateway (TGW).
  2. Add routes in the Client VPN Endpoint Route Table targeting each destination VPC CIDR.
  3. Update the VPC Route Table of the associated subnet to forward traffic across the peering connection or Transit Gateway attachment.
  4. Add corresponding Authorization Rules granting the required groups permission to each destination CIDR.
6. What happens if an entire AWS Availability Zone experiences an outage?

If your Client VPN endpoint is associated with target subnets across two or more Availability Zones (e.g., us-east-1a and us-east-1b), the service provides automated multi-AZ resilience:

  • The endpoint monitors the health of the underlying subnet network interfaces.
  • If us-east-1a degrades, traffic is automatically routed through the healthy network interface in us-east-1b.
  • New client connections are automatically assigned to the operational Availability Zone.
7. Does AWS Client VPN support IPv6?

AWS Client VPN currently supports IPv4 traffic only:

  • The Client CIDR block must be an IPv4 range (between /22 and /12).
  • Target network associations, routes, and authorization rules must be defined using IPv4 CIDR blocks.
8. How is AWS Client VPN priced, and how can we optimize costs?

AWS Client VPN billing consists of two components:

  1. Endpoint Association Fee: Fixed hourly rate per associated subnet (~$0.10/hour per subnet association = ~$73/month per AZ association).
  2. Client Connection Fee: Hourly fee per active connected client session (~$0.05/hour per active connection).
9. How do we execute an emergency offboarding of an employee?
  • If using SAML 2.0 (SSO): Immediately disable or delete the user's account in your corporate Identity Provider (Okta / Microsoft Entra ID). Terminate active sessions via AWS CLI: 
    aws ec2 terminate-client-vpn-connections \
    --client-vpn-endpoint-id cvpn-endpoint-xxxx \
    --connection-id cvpn-connection-xxxx
  • If using Mutual TLS (mTLS): Generate a Certificate Revocation List (CRL) containing the client certificate's serial number, and import the CRL to the Client VPN endpoint.

docs.title: Cost Optimization Strategies:
docs.text:
• Consolidate Endpoints: Instead of creating separate endpoints for Dev, QA, Staging, and Production, deploy a single shared endpoint and use group-based Authorization Rules to segment access.
  • Multi-AZ Association Balance: Associate 2 subnets for production workloads (high availability); single-AZ association may suffice for non-critical development sandbox environments.
  • Enforce Idle Timeouts: Configure session timeouts (e.g. 8–10 hours) so inactive connections do not run indefinitely overnight.

docs.title: Applied OSI Model in AWS Client VPN
Overview
docs.text:
The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) reference model characterizes computing and telecommunication functions into seven abstract layers. Rather than treating this purely as academic theory, an enterprise network architect must understand how AWS Client VPN operates across each specific layer of the OSI model.

![OSI 7 Layers](assets/OSI-7-layers.png)

docs.title: AWS Client VPN Layer-by-Layer Mapping
docs.text:
AWS Client VPN is an implementation of the OpenVPN protocol operating across the OSI stack:

flowchart TD
    L7["Layer 7: Application<br/>HTTPS, SSH, RDP payload + SAML 2.0 Auth"]
    L6["Layer 6: Presentation<br/>TLS 1.2 / 1.3 Encryption (AES-256-GCM)"]
    L5["Layer 5: Session<br/>OpenVPN session state, keepalives, renegotiation"]
    L4_Inner["Layer 4: Transport (Inner Payload)<br/>User TCP/UDP streams destined for VPC workloads"]
    L3_Inner["Layer 3: Network (Inner Payload)<br/>Client CIDR IP routing (172.16.0.45 to 10.0.1.50)"]
    L4_Outer["Layer 4: Transport (Carrier Tunnel)<br/>UDP Port 1194 (Preferred) OR TCP Port 443"]
    L3_Outer["Layer 3: Network (Carrier)<br/>Public Internet IP routing between client ISP and AWS endpoint"]
    L2["Layer 2: Data Link<br/>Point-to-point TUN virtual network adapter"]
    L1["Layer 1: Physical<br/>Fiber, 5G/Wi-Fi, and AWS global backbone physical cabling"]

    L7 --> L6 --> L5 --> L4_Inner --> L3_Inner --> L4_Outer --> L3_Outer --> L2 --> L1

docs.title: Layer 3 TUN vs Layer 2 TAP Architecture
docs.text:
OpenVPN and VPN protocols typically support two virtual network driver modes:

Dimension Layer 3: TUN (Routing) Layer 2: TAP (Bridging) Operating Layer Network Layer (IP packets) Data Link Layer (Ethernet frames) AWS Client VPN Support Standard (Exclusively supported) Prohibited / Not supported Broadcast / Multicast Does not forward broadcast (efficient) Forwards all broadcasts (high network noise) Payload Overhead Lower overhead (only raw IP packets) Higher overhead (includes full 14-byte Ethernet headers) Enterprise Fit Ideal for IP routing across VPCs, peered networks, and on-premises Used primarily for legacy protocols requiring raw Ethernet bridging

TUN Adapter Behavior

AWS Client VPN operates in Layer 3 TUN mode. Clients install a virtual TUN adapter on their operating system. When the VPN connection is established, the OS routing table redirects packets matching the target network routes into the TUN device, where they are encapsulated and encrypted.

docs.title: The Layer 4 Transport Dilemma: UDP 1194 vs TCP 443
docs.text: AWS Client VPN supports both UDP and TCP as the carrier protocol on ports 443 and 1194.

docs.title: Why UDP 1194 is Strongly Recommended (Avoiding TCP-in-TCP Meltdown)
docs.text:
When users run TCP-based applications (such as HTTPS, SSH, database queries, or git clones) over a VPN tunnel that is itself running on TCP (e.g. TCP port 443), an architectural phenomenon known as TCP-over-TCP meltdown can occur:

flowchart LR
    subgraph Client ["Client Device"]
        InnerTCP["Inner TCP Stream<br/>(Application Payload)"]
        OuterTCP["Outer TCP Stream<br/>(VPN Tunnel Carrier)"]
    end

    InnerTCP --> OuterTCP
    OuterTCP -->|Network Packet Drop| PacketLoss["Packet Loss on Public Internet"]
    PacketLoss -->|Retransmission 1| OuterTCP
    PacketLoss -->|Duplicate Retransmission 2| InnerTCP
    InnerTCP -.-> Bottleneck["Congestion Collapse and Meltdown<br/>Connection Freezes"]
  1. If a packet is dropped on the public internet, the outer TCP layer pauses and retransmits the lost packet.
  2. Simultaneously, the inner application TCP layer detects missing packets and begins its own independent retransmissions and exponential backoff timers.
  3. The two independent TCP sliding window algorithms fight each other, creating a queue backlog that leads to catastrophic throughput drops and dropped connections.
  4. Resolution: Running over UDP port 1194 avoids this conflict completely because UDP provides connectionless transport, allowing the inner application's TCP stack to handle retransmissions cleanly without double-buffering.

docs.title: When to Use TCP 443
docs.text: The only valid scenario for TCP 443 is when remote engineers are connecting from restrictive guest Wi-Fi networks (hotels, airports, or client corporate networks) that block outbound UDP traffic entirely. In that case, TCP 443 masquerades as standard outbound HTTPS traffic.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: A subnet is a distinct IP address range within an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC). Subnets enable network engineers to logically partition cloud infrastructure across physical Availability Zones (AZs), ensuring high availability, fault isolation, and precise traffic segmentation.

docs.title: Subnet Architecture for AWS Client VPN
docs.text:
When configuring AWS Client VPN, subnets serve as the Target Networks where the Client VPN endpoint attaches managed Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs). Understanding subnet constraints is essential to preventing production outages.

flowchart LR
    subgraph AZ_A ["Availability Zone: us-east-1a"]
        SubnetA["Client VPN Association Subnet A<br/>10.0.10.0/28<br/>(Primary Association)"]
        AppA["App Subnet A<br/>10.0.1.0/24"]
    end

    subgraph AZ_B ["Availability Zone: us-east-1b"]
        SubnetB["Client VPN Association Subnet B<br/>10.0.11.0/28<br/>(Redundant Association)"]
        AppB["App Subnet B<br/>10.0.2.0/24"]
    end

    Endpoint["AWS Client VPN Endpoint"] --> SubnetA
    Endpoint --> SubnetB
    SubnetA -.-> AppA
    SubnetB -.-> AppB

docs.title: Technical Rules & Constraints for Client VPN Subnets
1. Same VPC Restriction
docs.text: All subnets associated with a given Client VPN endpoint must reside within the same VPC. You cannot associate Subnet A from vpc-1 and Subnet B from vpc-2 to the same endpoint. Multi-VPC connectivity is achieved via VPC Peering or AWS Transit Gateway.

docs.title: 2. One Subnet per Availability Zone
docs.text:
AWS Client VPN enforces a strict limitation: You can associate only one subnet per Availability Zone.

  • Allowed: Subnet in us-east-1a + Subnet in us-east-1b
  • Prohibited: Two distinct subnets both located in us-east-1a

docs.title: 3. Sizing & IP Address Allocation
docs.text:
AWS requires target subnets to have a minimum CIDR block size of /27 (recommended) or /28:

  • A /28 subnet provides 16 IP addresses.
  • AWS reserves 5 addresses (.0, .1, .2, .3, .255), leaving 11 usable IP addresses.
  • Client VPN creates managed network interfaces in the target subnet to handle client traffic. Having sufficient headroom prevents ENI allocation failures during traffic spikes or scaling events.

Subnet IP Exhaustion Risk

If you associate a heavily utilized existing application subnet (e.g., where EKS pods or Lambda functions consume almost all private IPs), Client VPN will fail to provision its required scaling ENIs, leading to failed client connection attempts.

Best Practice: Provision dedicated, isolated subnets specifically for Client VPN associations.

docs.title: Sizing Comparison Table
docs.text: Metric Subnet /28 Subnet /27 Subnet /24 Total IPs 16 32 256 AWS Reserved 5 5 5 Usable IPs 11 27 251 Suitability for VPN Suitable for small deployments Recommended for Production Over-provisioned (unless shared with compute)

docs.title: High Availability & Multi-AZ Resilience
docs.text:
By associating subnets across at least two Availability Zones:

  1. Automated Redundancy: If a single Availability Zone experiences a hardware degradation or service disruption, the Client VPN service automatically routes client traffic through the healthy AZ association without administrative intervention.
  2. Bandwidth Scaling: Associating multiple subnets distributes the throughput load across multiple AWS-managed network interfaces, preventing bottlenecking on a single physical link.
